<reason>A very close, high-quality debate. CON (A) built a genuinely strong threshold mechanism ("loneliness in a crowd") and answered the cost-contradiction pressure credibly with amortization across group sessions and courses; its closing reframe—spend the marginal dollar on what is missing, not on abundant rooms—was sharp. But PRO (B) landed the debate's decisive pressure question ("expecting them where?"), and CON's answer largely pointed back to existing libraries and cafés, which PRO converted into "an app that succeeds by sending people to a library is an argument for the library." PRO also pre-empted CON's "rooms already exist and are empty" line by explaining that rooms are underused at 2 p.m. because the lonely are at work and branches lock the door at the hour loneliness peaks—CON never engaged that 6–9 p.m. point. PRO's category charge that CON stretched "app-based interventions" into telehealth also kept CON tethered to a partly swapped motion. PRO suffered real execution costs (two clipped turns, and an uncharitable "one clinician per user" characterization that CON exposed), and CON's homebound argument stayed live, which keeps the margin thin. On balance PRO made the choice slightly easier to decide as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q2/closing sequence: "expecting them where?" forced CON to list destinations that were either the existing library or paid venues, letting PRO recast CON's intervention as a pointer whose success depends on the very rooms the motion funds; CON's "fund more signs, not a second road" reply was clever but conceded the road matters and never addressed why the rooms are locked at the hours the lonely could use them.</best_rebuttal>
